lines: In 1977, a rocket sent Voyager 2 on its
way toward Jupiter.
On its own, that launch wasn't enough
to escape.
Without Jupiter, its path would have
curved back toward the Sun,
never getting much farther out than
Jupiter's distance.
Instead, it bent at Jupiter. Then
at Saturn. Then Uranus. Then Neptune.
Today, it's in interstellar space.
So how can flying past a planet make a
spacecraft faster?
The answer depends on who's watching.
Let's watch from the planet first. In
this view,
Jupiter sits still.
Our spacecraft falls toward it, and speeds
up as it drops in.
It swings around, and starts climbing
back out.
And climbing out, it slows down again.
By the time it's clear, with no
engines firing,
it's moving about as fast as when it
arrived. Measured from Jupiter,
the flyby gave it no extra speed.
But something did change. Look at the
arrows. Same length.
Different direction.
That's the difference between speed
and velocity.
Speed is how fast. Velocity is how fast,
and which way.
The flyby left the speed alone. It turned
the velocity.
Now let's watch the same flyby from the
Sun. And here's what the first view hid:
Jupiter isn't standing still. It's moving
along its orbit.
The spacecraft still follows the same kind
of curve around Jupiter.
But now that curve is moving through space
with the planet.
Measured from Jupiter, the speed
didn't change.
Measured from the Sun, the spacecraft
leaves faster than it arrived.
Same flyby. Two answers. Both of
them right.
Here's why. Seen from the Sun, the
spacecraft's velocity is two arrows added
together. Jupiter's motion, plus the
spacecraft's motion relative to Jupiter.
During the flyby, Jupiter's arrow
barely changes.
The spacecraft's arrow keeps its length,
but turns.
Turned to point more along Jupiter's
motion, the two arrows add up to a longer
one. That longer arrow is the speed gain,
measured from the Sun.
So where does that extra energy come from?
Not from nowhere.
The spacecraft's gravity pulls on Jupiter
too. As the spacecraft gains orbital
energy, Jupiter gives up a tiny amount of
its own orbital energy.
Jupiter is so massive that the change is
almost imperceptible.
Its orbit carries on.
The spacecraft didn't make speed. It
borrowed it.
Which way it turns decides everything.
Pass behind a moving planet, and you can
leave faster,
relative to the Sun.
Pass in front of it, and the turn works
against you.
You leave slower.
So a flyby can be an accelerator, or a
brake. Galileo skimmed past Jupiter's moon
Io to shed energy, and saved ninety
kilograms of fuel.
Now for the real thing. In the
late nineteen-seventies,
the four giant planets drifted into a
favourable alignment,
one that comes around roughly once every
hundred and seventy-five years.
The alignment made a journey past all
four possible.
Voyager 2's trajectory kept that door
open. And it took it.
At Jupiter, its path bent toward Saturn.
At Saturn,
toward Uranus. At Uranus, toward Neptune,
which it reached in nineteen eighty-nine.
Its twin, Voyager 1, took a different
road. A close pass by Saturn's moon Titan
sent it away from any further
giant-planet encounters.
Measured from the Sun, those flybys more
than doubled Voyager 2's speed.
And that dashed path is where it would
have gone without them.
So if a planet can fling you out of the
Solar System,
falling into the Sun should be
easy. It's just falling, after all.
The catch: Earth is racing sideways around
the Sun at about thirty kilometres
a second. And so is everything we launch
from it.
Aim straight at the Sun, and that sideways
speed carries you right past it.
To fall in, you have to get rid of it.
That was the problem facing NASA's Parker
Solar Probe.
It needed to shed about fifty-three
thousand miles per hour of sideways speed.
So it used the brake. It flew past Venus
seven times.
Taken together, those flybys reduced its
orbital energy around the Sun,
letting its orbit reach closer and
closer in.
The last one came in November
twenty twenty-four.
Here's the twist. With its orbital
energy reduced,
Parker fell deep toward the Sun. On
Christmas Eve,
twenty twenty-four, it passed about six
million kilometres from the surface,
faster than anything humans have built.
It got there by slowing down first.
So here's the whole trick, in three
parts. One:
change your view. From the planet, a flyby
only turns you.
From the Sun, that turn can change
your speed.
Two: nothing is created. Orbital energy is
transferred between the spacecraft and
the planet.
Three: aim decides. Relative to the Sun,
pass behind,
and you speed up. Pass in front, and you
slow down.
Voyager 1 is still heading out. On the
eighteenth of November,
twenty twenty-six, it crosses the
one-light-day mark.
A message from home will take almost a day
to reach it.
